Convexity & Framework Integrity Scoring

The Execution Kernel

The framework, measured.

The first five Parts set out what the framework believes and how a portfolio gets built: the regime it expects, the thinkers it borrows from, the macro thesis, the account structure, and how each position is sized and governed. Part 6 adds the measurement rules: how the two scores are computed, what each penalty costs, and how often the loop runs. It does not change the construction rules of Part 4 or Part 5.

Rules that nobody measures drift into suggestions, so the framework measures two things. The (CIS) rates each position on its own. The (FIS) rates how those positions have been put together. Each question the two scores answer has one owning score, and a weekly routine reads both. Position quality comes first.

Key Insight

Responsibility boundaries. CIS measures position quality. FIS measures portfolio assembly. Part 6 measures and flags; it decides nothing. The decisions its measurements inform are governed by the rules of Part 4 and Part 5, which this part checks but never rewrites.

Position Quality

CIS: scoring the position, not the portfolio.

The Convexity Integrity Score is a 0–100 score for a single asset, and it answers one question.

How attractive is this position, right now, as a convex opportunity under radical uncertainty?

The canonical CIS is position-level and portfolio-context-free: the same position scores the same whatever else you hold and however concentrated the portfolio has become. There is one narrow exception, a fixed +3 on the carry sub-score for a return-of-capital preferred held as outside a known tax-advantaged account (about +0.75 CIS at the reference macro weight). CIS does not evaluate diversification, concentration or a position’s correlation with your other holdings. Any portfolio-aware logic belongs to FIS or governance, never to CIS.

Governance reads a wrapper-aware version, which the framework’s governance rules call for. The dashboard computes it by multiplying the canonical score by a factor between 0.97 and 1.04, set by the holding’s account and its , and rounding the result. This wrapper-adjusted CIS is the number shown beside each holding, and it is what the dashboard’s governance checks and its Next Dollar Score (its score for where new money goes) read. A position scoring 69.5 shows 72 in a Roth and 68 in a taxable account, on opposite sides of the 70 line. FIS reads the canonical score.

The score is built from four components, each asking a different question about the same position.

  1. Convexity & Optionality (C) · 40 percent

    measures headroom, optionality, catalyst density and scarcity, with headroom the largest of the four. It carries the largest share at the reference weights because is the framework’s objective function.

  2. Risk & Fragility (R) · 25 percent

    measures survivability under stress rather than price volatility: balance sheet, business-model fragility, factor correlation and tail exposure. A higher score means lower fragility.

  3. Macro Alignment (M) · 25 percent

    measures fit to the forces of the current regime: regime fit (40 points), (30) and policy and flow (30), read against the Part 2 thesis. The dashboard also tilts regime fit, policy and carry by a few points from the current direction of rates, inflation and unemployment; the Math page gives the rule.

  4. Execution & Sentiment (E) · 10 percent

    measures whether reality is starting to validate the thesis. For a stock that means execution quality, read from three-month price momentum with a volatility adjustment, and market acceptance, read from trading turnover (thirty-day dollar volume over market value), fifty points each; funds use expense ratio and assets, and Bitcoin and crypto have their own inputs. It carries the least weight because execution follows quality.

The 40/25/25/10 split is the reference weighting. When a thesis is active, its profile sets the weights (Fourth Turning runs 0.35/0.30/0.25/0.10), each within 0.10 of the reference, floored at 0.05, capped at 0.50 and renormalized to sum to 1.0. With no thesis selected, the dashboard does not pick one for you, and a score computed without a thesis profile uses the reference weights. Two adjustments are built in. When the macro read is low or medium confidence, the macro weight drops to 60 or 80 percent of its value and the difference moves evenly to convexity and risk. And a sector-relevance multiplier of 0.80 to 1.20 scales the convexity and macro component scores, damped toward 1.0 when the risk score is weak. The four-component structure itself is doctrine.

What CIS leaves out matters as much as what it includes. Each exclusion has a home elsewhere, and the table names it.

What CIS excludes, and where each concern belongs
Excluded from CIS Belongs to
Portfolio diversificationFIS (Concentration bucket)
Position sizingGovernance (Part 5)
Thematic overlap / crowdingGovernance (Part 5 sizing and concentration caps; not scored)
Internal correlationGovernance (detection only)
Tax efficiency / wrapper placementGovernance (Part 4)
Concentration limitsFIS (Concentration bucket; Part 5 sets the caps)

CIS answers one question about one asset · FIS scores concentration, correlation is a detect-only tripwire, the rest is governed by Parts 4 and 5

Mechanics 01 · Floats, not tiers

Continuous scoring.

The composite is carried as a float from end to end: a position scores 78.3, not 75 or 80. Some inputs are read off stepped ladders, such as the momentum and turnover tiers, but nothing rounds the stored score; the wrapper-adjusted number shown beside a holding is rounded to a whole number. Continuity preserves information. A score that can only land on round tiers hides small week-over-week movement, and small movement is what longitudinal tracking exists to see.

Mechanics 02 · Clamps applied live: ±3 / ±5 / ±8 · derived-proxy ±6

Delta clamping: how far a score may move.

Score updates are confidence-weighted, and each update is clamped to a bounded move: low confidence permits ±3 points, medium ±5, high ±8, and evidence derived through a proxy rather than observed directly ±6. A material thesis change widens the bound to ±15. A first score is not clamped, because there is nothing to measure it against. Three cases skip the clamp: a change in the scoring model’s version (for crypto, a change in the model that produced the prior score); a private position, which is scored on a separate structural path with no clamp; and any move larger than 20 points, which the dashboard treats as a model disagreement and lets through in full. At medium confidence a +10 update therefore moves the score 5 points, while a +21 update lands in full. The research, market-structure and filing adjustments and the coverage caps, described below, apply after the clamp.

Why clamp at all? A score fed by the news cycle swings with it, and without a limit one enthusiastic week could rewrite months of accumulated conviction. The clamp makes moderate re-ratings, up to 20 points, earn their way across successive updates; a larger jump passes through and is logged as a model divergence for you to inspect.

Nobody types in the confidence level. The dashboard derives it from the quality of the evidence behind each component and aggregates the result, with two caps: an unclassified over-the-counter listing caps at low confidence, and a company with a market value under $50 million at medium. That keeps CIS in the role of decision support: the score says how sure its evidence lets it be, and you decide what to do about it.

Mechanics 03 · Six scoring lanes · four archetype labels

Scoring routes: the lens fits the asset.

Structurally different assets cannot be scored honestly through one lens, so CIS routes each position to a scoring lane before it applies the rubric. There are six: Bitcoin, crypto, ETF, equity, private-structural and not-scorable. Separately, the dashboard labels each position with one of four structural archetypes (spot Bitcoin, ETF, levered ETF, or operating equity, the default); the label’s main job is in FIS, which leaves the Bitcoin archetype out of its concentration measures. The archetype is labeling; the route is the lens.

Bitcoin runs on a monetary-TAM path, because that is what it is: a scarcity claim on a monetary market rather than a business with a balance sheet. The score does not size, gate or sell it. Part 3’s rules govern it: accumulate only, at a pace set by valuation discipline, outside the three postures and the concentration limits. Funds score through the same size-convexity curve as equities, on the weighted-average market cap of what they hold instead of their own assets: a broad index fund lands in the curve’s low, mega-cap zone, while a niche fund of smaller names can reach its peak.

The archetype puts no floor under the number. The score is the weighted sum of the four components (after the sector-relevance scaling and macro-confidence downweight described above), followed by the delta clamp and a short, named cascade of bounded adjustments and ceilings: research and market-structure deltas, a coverage cap of 75, 68 or 60 when evidence is thin, an 85 cap when the score leans on proxies, and a filing-intelligence delta. Each is recorded in the score’s breakdown; the Math page walks the order. There is no cash-like archetype either: an asset held for stability is governed as Ballast under Part 5’s posture rules, not scored on a separate rubric here. The route sets the lens for what a position is in itself; portfolio context and relative allocation stay outside CIS entirely.

Mechanics 04 · The shared four-band register

Reading the number.

Scores fall into four bands, named here for reading. Seventy and above is Strong; 60 up to 70 is Moderate (so a 69.9 is Moderate); 50 up to 60 is Caution; below 50 is Weak. In the dashboard the same bands carry numeric labels (70+, 60–69, 50–59, ≤49) and conviction tiers (core, standard, starter, avoid); the Next Dollar Score’s strong, moderate and weak ladder cuts at different points, so read the two separately.

<50Weak50–59Caution60–69Moderate70+Strong

This register is shared: in the dashboard, CIS and FIS read these same four bands. On FIS, 70 is the action line; on CIS, it is the Strong band’s floor, a band boundary, not an action trigger. That covers the position. The other half of the kernel scores the assembly.

Construction Integrity

FIS: good positions can create bad portfolios.

Ten positions that each score well can still add up to a bad portfolio: three of them half the book, nearly all of it in one kind of account, and half the money riding on theses nobody wrote down. The Framework Integrity Score exists to catch that. It measures how well the portfolio is assembled against the framework’s rules.

The scoring direction · 100 minus named penalties

Subtractive scoring: every lost point has an owner.

FIS starts the assembled portfolio at 100 and deducts capped, named penalties in five buckets: allocation (25), governance (15), dead capital (15), concentration (15) and complexity (10, hard cap). The caps sum to 80, so a valid FIS cannot fall below 20. The direction matters. A score built by addition invites argument about what deserves credit; a score built by subtraction has to name names. Every point below 100 traces to a specific departure from a specific rule, so the score reads as a repair list. Fix the violation and the points come back once the score can see the fix. FIS does not restate the rules it measures; where it uses a threshold of its own, the table below says so.

Two buckets scale with position size. Governance and dead-capital charges are multiplied by the position’s share of the portfolio, counted between 0.2 and 12 percent: a 6-point charge on a 5 percent position costs 0.3 points, and no single position can cost more than 0.72 in governance or 0.84 in dead capital. Allocation, concentration and complexity charges are flat.

The mechanism is easiest to see run once. The exhibit below walks an example portfolio down from 100, one deduction per bucket, to the 83 it earns, in the Strong band.

The deductions in the exhibit are illustrative. The table below sets out the framework’s FIS rules: the buckets, their caps and what each one charges. The dashboard computes them, but its score does not yet see every input: nothing sets the momentum-breakdown flag, and the thesis, distribution-type, hold-rationale, remediation-plan and override records you keep on a holding are not passed to the score, so a holding can be charged as undocumented or unclassified even when those records exist.

The five FIS penalty buckets, their caps, and what each one charges
Bucket Max penalty What it charges
Allocation25 ptsThe aggregate dollar split across Roth, taxable and pre-tax, measured against the FIS wrapper targets of 45/35/20% and charged only once total drift passes 10 points (worth at most about 6 points), plus the count-based spread of positions across score bands (up to 5 points per band line; a band’s drift of 2 points or less costs nothing). It does not check whether each asset sits in the wrapper Part 4 assigns it.
Governance15 ptsOne charge per position, first match wins: a score below 60 (6) · a position in the 60s weighing more than 8% of the portfolio (6) · any other position in the 60s (4) · momentum breakdown (4; specified, but nothing in the dashboard sets it yet). Value-weighted.
Dead capital15 ptsNo documented thesis (5) · a score older than 90 days (2). Value-weighted.
Concentration15 ptsEach position above 15% (8 each), matching Part 5’s default cap · top three above 40% (6) and top five above 60% (4), looser than Part 5’s 35% and 50% · Bitcoin excluded by archetype. By the FIS rules a breach under a documented override is marked as acknowledged; the dashboard’s score does not yet read overrides, and the points apply either way.
Complexity10 pts (hard cap)Unclassified distributions (1 each) · positions scoring below 70 carried without documented rationale, beyond an allowance of three (0.5 each). By the FIS rules a documented thesis, hold rationale or remediation plan suppresses the low-score charge; the dashboard’s score does not yet read those records.

Five buckets · caps sum to 80 · each charge names the rule it measures

The floor of 20 is only a bound. Value weighting keeps governance and dead capital each under 10 points for any book of fewer than 200 positions, so a portfolio of that size that breaks every rule still scores above 30.

Two accounting notes. Tax architecture is not a separate bucket. The score measures the aggregate wrapper mix, not per-asset placement, so Part 4’s placement rules stay your check: a book holding Torque that may rotate in taxable and return-of-capital Ballast in a Roth draws no wrapper penalty if its dollar split sits near 45/35/20. The 45/35/20 targets are FIS’s own parameters: Part 4 sets no fixed split, so a book routed by its sequence, with little or no pre-tax, shows some wrapper drift here. Bitcoin held under the dashboard’s own Bitcoin wrapper counts toward the total but has no target, so it adds to the measured drift.

is not a score bucket either. The dashboard reports it alongside the score, measured in percentage points against the posture targets derived from your operating thesis (or a fixed default when no thesis is active) instead of the Part 5 ranges. Its diagnostics warn at 10 points or more and fail at 20, and its Framework Rule Register grades the same drift on the framework’s governance ladder of 5, 10 and 15 points.

FIS reads the shared four-band register; the band prescribes the action
FIS range Band Action
70–100StrongMaintain; optimize when convenient
60–69ModerateWatch; review attribution, prioritize the top penalty
50–59CautionActive remediation; pause new positions
<50WeakComprehensive repair; pause new positions

The same register CIS reads · on FIS, 70 is the action line · the band prescribes urgency, the attribution prescribes the fix

In the dashboard, FIS below 70 produces a fix-the-top-penalty recommendation when you run the Weekly Review, and below 60 the three-level check (described with the weekly workflow below) raises a framework-breach review with a 24-hour deadline. Neither blocks a trade.

One score for the position, one for the assembly, both read against the same register. The diagnosis comes from reading them together.

Two Scores, One Diagnosis

Neither score compensates for the other.

CIS never reads FIS. FIS reads CIS only through its four bands: positions below 70 draw governance charges, the count of positions in each band feeds the Allocation bucket, and undocumented positions below 70 count toward Complexity. Conviction therefore shows up in FIS as unresolved governance. Under the FIS rules, twenty equal-weight positions scoring 65, each documented, with its distributions classified and the book on its wrapper targets, still lose 14 points (4 governance, 10 band distribution) and score 86. A 95-CIS position does not offset a poorly assembled book, and a well-assembled book does not lift a 65-CIS position.

Each score calls for its own response. The dividing line on both is 70: the floor of the Strong band on each score, and on FIS also the action line. Crossing the two at that line gives four states. The framework prescribes a response for each, and a repair order where both fall short.

CIS × FIS diagnosis and the prescribed action for each state
CIS FIS Diagnosis Action
Strong band (70+)Action line met (70+)HealthyMaintain
Strong band (70+)Remediation required (<70)Construction issueRepair wrappers, sizing and concentration; keep the positions
Below Strong (<70)Action line met (70+)Sub-core convictionHonor the posture-specific band; strengthen evidence, resize, or replace only as warranted
Below Strong (<70)Remediation required (<70)ComprehensiveRepair FIS first (compounds faster), then reassess and size each position by its CIS band

Construction failures compound faster than conviction shortfalls · when both sit below 70, repair construction first · exits stay reserved for scores below 50 or separately triggered governance

Score to size · The Weekly Review flags a 10-point move

How CIS feeds decisions.

CIS sizes a position within bands that Part 5 defines; it does not set the bands. Posture sets the band table and the score selects the band within it. Part 5’s Torque and Ballast sizing tables, and its Hype sizing rule (eligible from CIS 50, 2 to 5 percent per position under hard caps), carry the CIS-to-allocation mappings by posture. For Torque and Ballast, 70 or above supports core sizing, 60 to 69 standard sizing, 50 to 59 starter sizing (Ballast calls it marginal), and below 50 is not allocation-worthy.

CIS below 50 removes allocation eligibility: every posture’s band is zero, so the position takes no new capital and is exited or replaced, and reclassifying its posture does not restore eligibility. At 50 and above, exits are governed by posture rules, tripwires and thesis evidence, not by the score band alone. Three signals govern the response to score movement.

  1. Promotion: CIS rises 10 points or more

    The Weekly Review flags a move of 10 points or more since the last review and recommends resizing toward the band the new score earns. The pacing is yours: scale over two to four weeks rather than at once.

  2. Demotion: CIS falls 10 points or more

    The same signal flags a downsize toward the band the lower score earns, on the same pacing. A falling score narrows the band; above 50 it does not by itself force an exit.

  3. Posture reclassification: never by CIS alone

    A CIS change never changes posture. Part 5 bars reclassifying Hype as Torque to avoid a stop-loss; other posture moves are your judgment.

Signals only help if someone reads them on a schedule. The framework sets one.

The Operating Cadence

The weekly workflow.

The framework runs on a weekly pass, Sunday evening or Monday before the open: update CIS, calculate FIS, run the governance checks, act or deliberately hold, and log. Event-triggered updates fill the days between passes, and the pass is logged whether or not anything traded.

In the dashboard you run that pass from the Weekly Review page, which marks itself due seven days after the last completed review; nothing runs it on a schedule. It first asks the scoring pipeline to refresh a bounded set of stale scores, at most 10 per review: any score 30 or more days old or never computed, and any score 7 or more days old on a position of at least 2 percent of the book (1 percent when the score is low-confidence). Scores you have overridden are never refreshed. It then reads CIS, noting what changed since the last review, reads FIS, runs the governance checks, recommends actions by precedence and logs the review. It computes neither score itself.

The pass · Doctrine stations, run on demand

What each station does.

In doctrine the CIS station recomputes C, R, M and E for every position; in the dashboard the refresh is budgeted, and the review reports what changed. The FIS station totals the penalties across the five buckets and ranks the attribution for repair. The governance station then checks earnings proximity (positions above 3 percent; the dashboard counts calendar days, the doctrine five trading days), momentum, tripwires and posture drift.

Momentum here means Part 5’s three dimensions: distance from the 52-week high, strength against the sector and the market, and breadth. The dashboard does not yet measure these three dimensions. Its Momentum Death tripwire, meant to fire when all three break, reports unavailable rather than guessing. A coded screen of price against the 200-day and 50-day moving averages with an RSI band of 30 to 70 receives no data, so it reports every position as unavailable, and it is not treated as a stand-in for the three dimensions. What the dashboard does watch is stress across your holdings as a group, through the cohort confluence tripwire Part 5 describes.

Action then follows a fixed precedence. In doctrine a tripwire demands a response first; then an earnings window above the 3 percent cap; then FIS below 70 (fix the top penalty); then a CIS move of 10 points or more (resize). No trigger means hold. The Weekly Review ranks its recommendations the same way, except that first place goes to a finding from the dashboard’s three-level check. It also records where each of the framework’s tripwires stands, but those readings raise no recommendation of their own. And it cannot yet raise the earnings step, because it receives no earnings dates; the dashboard flags that case outside the review, in its Framework Rule Register and on the positions table.

The three-level check runs with every portfolio recompute and in the Weekly Review: level one flags any position whose wrapper-adjusted CIS is below 75, level two a sector where more than half the scored positions sit below 80, and level three an FIS below 60 (on a recompute, also three or more of its broader rule checks failing at once). None is an exit signal and none trades. In the Weekly Review each becomes a top-precedence recommendation, so a holding whose wrapper-adjusted score sits between 70 and 75 draws one every time you run it, even though it sits in the Strong band.

Logging closes the pass. The decision log keeps the last 52 reviews, a year at a weekly cadence. It records the positions whose scores changed, the FIS reading, the recommendations made or held back and why, or why none was needed; the Logbook and the governance audit page carry the qualitative record.

Interrupts · Four doctrine triggers, one detected

Intra-week triggers.

Four events interrupt the cadence instead of waiting for it: a position moving more than 5 percent in a single day · material news · an earnings announcement · a CIS update from new research. A tripwire interrupts by definition. The dashboard detects only the first, at 5 percent or more, after each quote refresh, and lists it on its Governance page as detected, not yet evaluated. Nothing evaluates it mid-week; acting on it is yours.

Between triggers, frequency limits keep you from confusing activity with diligence.

Action-frequency limits and their exceptions
Action type Minimum interval Exception
CIS recalculation7 days per positionMaterial news event
Position addition3 days between addsEarnings rebuild
Full exitNo limitTripwire triggered
Partial trim5 days between trimsEarnings proximity

Exits are never rate-limited when a tripwire fires · the dashboard holds back a repeat resize recommendation for 5 days and does not refresh a score younger than 7 days; the add interval is yours to keep

The Restraint Principle

Restraint is part of the method. A CIS change under 5 points: monitor. An FIS change under 5 points: monitor. A position whose size already sits inside the band its score earns: no resize. All governance checks pass: hold. A week in which everything was measured and nothing moved is the system working.

The cadence earns its keep less in the weeks it acts than in what happens when it stops running.

Failure Modes

How implementations decay unnoticed.

Implementations rarely fail loudly. They degrade through patterns that send no obvious signal: a score nobody re-ran, an allocation the market moved without a single trade, a tax leak too small to notice in any given month. The exhibit below sketches what those patterns do to a healthy portfolio in the year after reviews stop.

The framework watches five patterns, each with a diagnostic: a threshold that turns a slow, invisible failure into an explicit flag. The Weekly Review runs all five diagnostics when you start it. Four can fire; correlation stacking has no input yet, so correlation is watched by a portfolio tripwire instead. Staleness, posture drift and large unrefreshed gains are also checked outside the review by the dashboard’s framework diagnostics.

Slow CIS decay

A position that scored 82 eighteen months ago may deserve a 68 today (the thesis played out, the TAM compressed, the catalysts ran out), but without a recalculation its size stays put. Diagnostic: a score older than 90 days is stale; the dead-capital bucket charges it 2 base points, value-weighted, and the dashboard’s diagnostics warn once a score is more than 60 days old and fail past 90.

Silent posture drift

Markets move posture weights without a single trade: Torque runs from 55 to 70 percent of the book and Ballast falls underweight. Diagnostic: the dashboard warns when a posture sits 10 percentage points or more from its target and fails at 20, so this 15-point drift draws a warning. The warning opens a review, and the review decides. The framework rejects mechanical rebalancing, on a calendar or back to fixed percentage bands (Part 5), and nothing trades on its own.

Wrapper inefficiency accumulation

Positions land in whichever account had cash that day. Each misplacement looks minor, and the cost compounds for decades; Part 4 works the arithmetic for a gain realized once, and Part 5 for gains realized every year. Diagnostic: the Allocation bucket bills the account-level split against its targets as one aggregate line. It does not flag a single asset held in the wrong wrapper, so naming misplaced positions stays your job.

Correlation stacking

CIS scores positions one at a time, and regime stress makes them move together. Five AI-infrastructure positions can each score 85 and still fall as one trade when liquidity drains. Diagnostic: the Correlation Spike tripwire flags average pairwise correlation above 0.70, computed from your holdings’ daily closes once every holding has at least 60 daily returns. The flag is informational: no FIS bucket charges for correlation, CIS never does, and no action is forced; the doctrine’s response, adding uncorrelated assets, is yours.

Overconfidence via narrative reinforcement

A big gain makes the thesis feel truer just when the market may already have paid for it. Diagnostic: a position more than 50 percent above its cost basis whose score is older than 60 days is flagged for a refresh.

Without recalculation, the story substitutes for current analysis. Each of these failures still rounds to healthy on any single day and shows up only in week-over-week tracking, so framework health has to be read as a trend. The last question is what carries that tracking in practice.

Framework Completion

A complete system, run weekly.

The six Parts form one system. The framework sets the rules; you carry them out. The weekly work is concrete: review CIS for every position, recalculate FIS after portfolio changes, watch the earnings calendar, track momentum, check posture drift, evaluate tripwires, and keep the longitudinal record. None of it is hard on its own. All of it has to happen, every week, for the measurements to mean anything.

Three implementation paths carry that work.

  1. Manual tracking

    Spreadsheets and a weekly routine. Workable for a portfolio of fewer than 10 positions, and prone to drift as it grows.

  2. Custom tooling

    Your own CIS and FIS calculations, with alerts. Works if you can build it and will keep maintaining it.

  3. The ACF Dashboard

    The framework running as software. It computes delta-clamped CIS and the five-bucket FIS with attribution, runs an on-demand Weekly Review with decision logging, and flags tripwires: the framework’s position and portfolio tripwires, a cohort confluence tripwire, and a three-level check whose findings are review prompts with 7-day, 14-day and 24-hour deadlines. The Weekly Review runs the five failure-mode diagnostics above when you start it; four can fire, and correlation is watched by its tripwire instead. The dashboard records every trade, never blocks one and places no orders.

Pick the one you will keep running for decades. The framework does not care which, only that the loop runs.

Product Scoring Extensions (Not Core Doctrine)

The dashboard also carries product-level scoring layers, the Framework Fit page and the Doctrine Audit, which build on CIS and FIS to answer product questions such as “which doctrine does this portfolio express?” They sit outside the CIS and FIS doctrine defined above and are evaluated and versioned separately. The Framework Fit page is switched off by default and, when enabled, runs only on synthetic sample books; the same scoring logic powers the Doctrine Audit, which can evaluate pasted holdings or the current portfolio offline when you ask it to.

Scope

This framework does not constitute investment, tax, or legal advice. Consult qualified professionals for your specific situation. The framework is a designed process, not a fitted model. Its rules and scores have not been backtested against a benchmark; where these pages describe outcomes, they describe what the design intends unless a figure is labeled as measured. Descriptions of what the dashboard does are as of September 2026.

End of Part 6

CIS rates each position on its own, and FIS rates how the positions fit together by charging each departure from the rules. Every week, read both, run the governance checks, act on a trigger or deliberately hold, and log the result. With measurement, flags and a cadence in place, the rules of the first five Parts become a working routine, and the framework is complete.
